rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet shares ordinary human nature with his audience; revelation is what distinguishes him and answers demands for what no human can do.
rows.anchor: لا أدعي الإحاطة بكلماته جل وعلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first restriction is a reversal aimed at hearers who treat his humanity as incompatible with prophethood or revelation.
rows.anchor: من قصر الموصوف على الصفة قصر قلب والمقصور عليه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view limits the Prophet to receiving revelation of this truth, against claims that he receives no revelation.
rows.anchor: مقصور على إيحاء ذلك إليه لا يتجاوزه إلى عدم الإيحاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second restriction says the true object of worship is one, with no plurality in divinity; it restricts the described object to oneness.
rows.anchor: أي معبودكم الحق والمقصور على الوحدانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects making this restriction one of attribute to object: adding ilāh prepares for wāḥid and clarifies unity in divinity; oneness cannot sensibly be shared by multiple objects. Restriction of specification is possible but ill-suited.
rows.anchor: فزيادة إله للتوطئة للوصف بواحد والإشارة إلى أن المراد الوحدة في الألوهية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rajāʾ primarily means hoping for future pleasure, but can also mean fear, as poetry attests.
rows.anchor: الرجاء طمع حصول ما فيه مسرة في المستقبل ويستعمل بمعنى الخوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Meeting the Lord may image the final outcome—death, resurrection, accounting, and recompense—like a servant returning to a master who knows his deeds.
rows.anchor: مثل للوصول إلى العاقبة من تلقي ملك الموت والبعث والحساب والجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings make meeting a metonym for resurrection, meeting the Lord’s reward, or seeing God on Judgment Day while He is pleased.
rows.anchor: اللقاء على حقيقته والكلام على حذف مضاف أيضا أي من كان يؤمل لقاء ثواب ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rajāʾ may mean fear of a bad encounter or recompense, but Alusi prefers hope and takes the expected gift to be God’s favor and glad tidings.
rows.anchor: وتفسير الرجاء بالطمع أولى وكذا كون المرجو الكرامة والبشرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The perfect verb signals continuing hope; such hope calls for good work suited to the expected favor.
rows.anchor: للدلالة على أن اللائق بحال العبد الاستمرار والاستدامة على رجاء الكرامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition covers open idolatry and hidden association, such as showing off or seeking worldly gain; Ibn Jubayr restricts it to ostentation, as does a report from al-Hasan, and hadith calls this minor shirk.
rows.anchor: ولا يشرك بعبادة ربه أحدا ﴾ إشراكا جليا

rows.speaker: جندب بن زهير
rows.claim: Jundub told the Prophet that he worked for God but felt pleased when seen; the Prophet said God does not accept work shared with another, and the verse confirmed the answer.
rows.anchor: جندب بن زهير قال لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : إني أعمل العمل لله تعالى

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: In a report from the Prophet conveying God’s words, God calls Himself the best partner and disowns work in which another is associated with Him.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يرويه عن ربه تعالى أنه قال

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: The Prophet says deeds are presented in sealed records at Judgment; although angels attest to good, God rejects work done for other than His sake.
rows.anchor: عن أنس قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم تعرض أعمال بني آدم

rows.speaker: يحيى بن الوليد بن عبادة
rows.claim: The Prophet says a person who campaigns with no aim beyond gaining a tether receives only what he intended.
rows.anchor: عن يحيى بن الوليد بن عبادة أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : من غزا

rows.speaker: أبو أمامة
rows.claim: Asked about a campaigner seeking reward and reputation, the Prophet repeatedly answers that he gets nothing, then says God accepts only sincere work seeking His face; Alusi calls the chain good.
rows.anchor: عن أبي أمامة قال : جاء رجل إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ghazali distinguishes pure sincerity, wholly ostentatious work, and sincerity interrupted by ostentation; ostentation after completion does not invalidate the deed, though conspicuous delight may raise concern.
rows.anchor: أن ينعقد من أوله إلى آخره على الإخلاص من غير شائبة رياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When ostentation enters before completion and motivates or influences the work, it spoils the part it accompanies and can invalidate what preceded it; this is the case relevant here.
rows.anchor: فإن كان باعثا له على العمل ومؤثرا فيه فسد ما قارنه وأحبطه ثم سرى إلى ما قبله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report through al-Suddi al-Saghir says Jundub increased prayer, fasting, or almsgiving when praised; the verse was revealed about him, and such work is invalidated.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال : كان جندب بن زهير إذا صلى أو صام أو تصدق

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A man told the Prophet that he did good work, was seen, and felt pleased; the Prophet promised two rewards, for secrecy and publicity.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة رضي الله تعالى عنه أن رجلا قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi explains the double reward when public visibility encourages imitation or another benefit, and pleasure concerns that good rather than vanity; the Prophet knew each questioner’s circumstances.
rows.anchor: إذا كان ظهور عمله لأحد باعثا على عمل مثله والاقتداء به فيه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the verse was revealed about polytheists who worshipped another god, not believers; Alusi finds an overt-shirk-only reading leaves the command then prohibition unexplained and prefers the general scope.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما أنه قال : أنزلت الآية في المشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paid Quran recitation for the dead earns neither the deceased nor the reciter any reward under the verse’s general prohibition.
rows.anchor: قراءة القرآن للموتى بالإجرة فلا ثواب فيها للميت ولا للقاريء أصلا

rows.speaker: علي بن موسى الرضا
rows.claim: A report says al-Rida told servants bringing water and a basin for prayer to prepare these himself, invoking the verse against seeking help even in worship; Alusi notes this broadens the prohibition to disliked as well as forbidden conduct.
rows.anchor: إن علي بن موسى الرضا رضي الله تعالى عنهما كان عند المأمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ most plausibly derives good work and avoidance of shirk from God’s unique divinity: the true God’s greatness and perfection call for both.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أن الفاء للتفريع على قصر الوحدانية عليه تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the alternative that good work follows from God’s divinity while avoiding shirk follows from oneness as an explanation for the command’s order; another view derives both from all that precedes.
rows.anchor: على ما روي عن ابن عباس وهو كما ترى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Replacing pronouns with the explicit title Lord reinforces the point and signals that lordship motivates compliance with the command and prohibition.
rows.anchor: ووضع الظاهر موضع الضمير في الموضعين مع التعرض لعنوان الربوبية

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: In al-Jaʿfi’s transmission, Abu ʿAmr reads the prohibition in second person, then shifts from address back to third person in b-rabbihi.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو في رواية الجعفي ( ولا تشرك ) بالتاء الفوقية

rows.speaker: معاوية بن أبي سفيان
rows.claim: A report from Muʿawiya calls this the final verse revealed, but Alusi says the truth is otherwise.
rows.anchor: وعن معاوية بن أبي سفيان أن هذه الآية ( فمن كان يرجو ) إلخ آخر آية نزلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Symbolic readings identify Dhul-Qarnayn with the heart or the complete spiritual master, and Gog and Magog with imagined impulses and inner whisperings.
rows.anchor: قيل ذو القرنين إشارة إلى القلب وقيل : إلى الشيخ الكامل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi rejects mapping the story’s outward geography onto inner faculties as an extremely strained allegory.
rows.anchor: وراموا التطبيق بين ما في الآفاق وما في الأنفس ولعمري لقد تكلفوا غاية التكلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He instead reads the story as instructing rulers to inspect their subjects, discipline wrongdoers, reward benefactors, aid the weak, prevent harm, and avoid coveting people’s property.
rows.anchor: الإشارة في القصة إلى إرشاد الملوك لاستكشاف أحوال رعاياهم وتأديب مسيئهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possible lesson in the story is that causes deserve consideration.
rows.anchor: وقد يقال : فيها إشارة إلى اعتبار الأسباب

rows.speaker: الأشاعرة
rows.claim: The Ashʿarites regard causes as unreal in themselves, illustrated by their shaykh’s claim that a blind person in China could see a place in Andalusia.
rows.anchor: وقال الأشاعرة : الأسباب في الحقيقة ملغاة

rows.speaker: السلف
rows.claim: The Salaf regard causes as relevant even though God’s acts do not logically depend on them.
rows.anchor: ومذهب السلف أنها معتبرة وإن لم يتوقف عليها فعل الله تعالى عقلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse about people who lose their worldly efforts while thinking they do good points to ostentatious people, including lodge-dwellers who court attention and ensnare the wealthy; they are exposed here and face expulsion and painful punishment in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى : ( الذين ضل سعيهم في الحياة الدنيا وهم يحسبون أنهم يحسنون صنعا ) إشارة إلى المرائين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi specifically includes those who sit in a lodge to attract public notice and ensnare worldly people through schemes.
rows.anchor: ومنهم الذين يجلسون في الخانقاه لأجل نظر الخلق وصرف وجوه الناس إليهم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report transmitted through al-Kalbi, Abu Salih, and Umm Hani glosses the letters as Kafi, Hadi, ʿAlim, and Sadiq.
rows.anchor: عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال كاف هاد عالم صادق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One Ibn Abbas report derives each letter from a divine name: Karim, Hadi, Hakim, ʿAlim, and Sadiq.
rows.anchor: كاف من كريم وها من هاد ويا من حكيم وعين من عليم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another Ibn Abbas report expands the letters as Kabir, Hadi, Amin, ʿAziz, and Sadiq.
rows.anchor: كبير هاد أمين عزيز صادق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Further reports call the sequence an oath by God and one of His names; another calls it the greatest divine name, supported by Ali’s use of it in prayer.
rows.anchor: هو قسم أقسم الله تعالى به وهو من أسماء الله تعالى

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Fatima bint Ali reports that Ali prayed, O Kāf-Hā-Yā-ʿAyn-Ṣād, forgive me; Alusi cites this to support the greatest-name interpretation.
rows.anchor: عن فاطمة بنت علي قالت : كان علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه : يقول يا كهيعص اغفر لي

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وناس من الصحابة
rows.claim: Ibn Masud and a group of Companions treat the letters as initials from divine names: King, God, Mighty, and Fashioner.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود وناس من الصحابة أنهم قالوا كهيعص هو الهجاء المقطع

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb gives a similar initial-letter gloss, omitting yāʾ and deriving ṣād from al-Ṣamad.
rows.anchor: عن محمد بن كعب نحو ذلك إلا أنه لم يذكر الياء وقال الصاد من الصمد

rows.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
rows.claim: Al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas interprets the letters as addressing the One who gives refuge and cannot be overpowered.
rows.anchor: عن الربيع بن أنس أنه قال في ذلك : يا من يجير ولا يجار عليه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada calls the letters one of the names of the Quran.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة أنه اسم من أسماء القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other views call the letters the name of the surah or a mere sequence recited by letter names; some researchers hold the latter, while some defer its reality to God.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنه اسم للسورة وعليه جماعة وقيل حروف مسرودة على نمط التعديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi points readers to his fuller discussion of such disjoint letters at the opening of al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم تمام الكلام في ذلك وأمثاله في أول سورة البقرة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers give kāf a still fāʾ; al-Hasan is reported with a rounded fāʾ, and Nafiʿ inclines the hāʾ alif between two pronunciations.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور كاف بإسكان الفاء وروي عن الحسن ضمها وأمال نافع هاويا

rows.speaker: الأكثرون
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce the dāl of ṣād clearly rather than assimilating it into the following dhāl; other reported variants round or incline hāʾ and yāʾ, while Hamza opens hāʾ and breaks yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وأظهر دال صاد ولم يدغمها في الذال بعد وعليه الأكثرون

rows.speaker: أبو الفضل الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi says the reported rounding is not literal ḍamma, which would change the following alif to wāw, but a Hijazi tendency of the alif toward wāw, opposite imala.
rows.anchor: قال أبو الفضل عبد الرحمن بن أحمد بن الحسن المقري الرازي في كتاب اللوامح : إن الضم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because these alifs lack an underlying origin, readers analogize them to alifs from wāw and yāʾ, permitting either tafkhim or imala.
rows.anchor: أن هذه الألفات لما لم يكن لها أصل حملوها على المنقلبة عن الواو تارة وعن الياء أخرى

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar separates the letters and stops on each; meeting two unvowelled sounds is tolerated in pause.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر بتقطيع هذه الحروف وتخليص بعضها من بعض

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu ʿAmr assimilates the dāl of ṣād into the following dhāl.
rows.anchor: وأدغم أبو عمرو دال صاد في الذال بعد

rows.speaker: حفص عن عاصم وفرقة
rows.claim: Hafs from Asim and a group pronounce the nūn of ʿayn clearly, while the majority conceal it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حفص عن عاصم وفرقة بإظهار النون من عين والجمهور على إخفائها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If each letter is a divine name, it has no syntactic case, individually or as a whole; another parse treats each letter as a completed predicate, or the first as complete and the rest as successive predicates.
rows.anchor: لا محل لشيء من ذلك ولا للمجموع من الإعراب

rows.speaker: الربيع
rows.claim: On al-Rabiʿ’s interpretation, the letters can be a vocative divine name meaning the One who gives refuge and cannot be overpowered.
rows.anchor: هو منادى وهو اسم من أسمائه تعالى معناه الذي يجير ولا يجار عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A proposed vocative word used to call God by that description, like mahayma in a question, strikes Alusi as far-fetched.
rows.anchor: وهو كلمة تقال في موضع نداء الله تعالى بذلك العنوان مثل ما يقال مهيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the sequence is simply a string of letter names, it has no syntactic case.
rows.anchor: وعلى القول بأنه حروف مسرودة على نمط التعديد قالوا : لا محل له من الإعراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Depending on the interpretation of the preceding letters, the phrase may predicate an omitted topic, identify the recited passage, or predicate the surah made from those letters.
rows.anchor: على هذه الأقوال خبر مبتدأ محذوف أي هذا المتلو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Kāf-Hā-Yā-ʿAyn-Ṣād names the surah, it can be pointed to as already present in discourse because it is on the verge of being mentioned.
rows.anchor: باعتبار كونه على جناح الذكر صار في حكم الحاضر المشاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr may be a predicate with an omitted topic or a subject with an omitted predicate; it may also mean that the title is the mention of the Lord’s mercy, since that opens and sums up the surah, or imply a possessive or passive construction.
rows.anchor: كونه مبتدأ خبره محذوف وقيل محله الرفع على أنه مبتدأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the title is Quran, it can denote the surah as part of the Quran or the whole Quran with the clause linked by inclusion, ellipsis, or interpretation.
rows.anchor: على القول بأنه اسم للقرآن قيل المراد بالقرآن ما يصدق على البعض ويراد به السورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAbdahu is the object of raḥma, a verbal noun governing its object because it is not a unit noun; alternatively it is the object of dhikr construed as a verbal noun by extension.
rows.anchor: مفعول لرحمة ربك على أنها مفعول لما أضيف إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr al-raḥma means that mercy reached and affected Zakariya, as when someone says a favor reached me.
rows.anchor: ومعنى ذكر رحمة ربك بلوغها وإصابتها كما يقال ذكرني معروفك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakariyya is parsed as a full appositive, an explanatory apposition, or an accusative with an implied I mean.
rows.anchor: بدل منه بدل كل من كل أو عطف بيان له أو نصب بإضمار أعني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idh may modify raḥma or dhikr, or be an appositive of inclusion to Zakariya, as in the passage about Maryam withdrawing to an eastern place.
rows.anchor: هو بدل اشتمال من ( زكريا ) كما قوله تعالى ( واذكر في الكتاب مريم إذ انتبذت

rows.speaker: الحسن وابن يعمر
rows.claim: They read dhakkara as an intensified past verb and raḥmata in the accusative; its first object is omitted, its second is mercy, and ʿabdahu is the object of mercy.
rows.anchor: قرأ الحسن وابن يعمر كما حكاه أبو الفتح ( ذكر ) فعلا ماضيا مشددا

rows.speaker: أبو الفتح
rows.claim: The subject of dhakkara may be the Quran from context, the disjoint letters construed as Quran, or God; people are the omitted object.
rows.anchor: وفاعل ( ذكر ) ضمير القرآن المعلوم من السياق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other parses make mercy the second object and ʿabdahu the first, or mercy the first and ʿabdahu the second; another takes the phrase metaphorically as God making mercy remember His servant.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون ( رحمة ربك ) مفعولا ثانيا والمفعول الأول هو ( عبده )

rows.speaker: أبو يعمر
rows.claim: Al-Dani reports Abu Yaʿmar reading an imperative: remind people of your Lord’s mercy toward Zakariya, directly or by means of that mercy.
rows.anchor: وذكر الداني عن أبي يعمر أنه قرأ ( ذكر ) على الأمر والتشديد

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi reads dhakara as a light past verb, raḥmata as its object, and ʿabdahu as its subject.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الكلبي ( ذكر ) فعلا ماضيا خفيفا و ( رحمة ربك ) بالنصب

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reports that Zakariya was the last prophet of the Children of Israel.
rows.anchor: وأخرج الحاكم وصححه عن ابن مسعود أنه آخر أنبياء بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that Zakariya was the son of Dan and one of the prophetic descendants who wrote revelation in Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن إسحاق بن بشر وابن عساكر عن ابن عباس أنه ابن دان

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A sound-graded report from Abu Hurayra says Zakariya was a carpenter.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة مرفوعا أنه عليه السلام كان نجارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakariya’s name has five forms: long and short forms read in the Seven, two forms of Zakari, and Zakar like qalam; it is foreign.
rows.anchor: وجاء في اسمه خمس لغات تولها المد وثانيها القصر وقريء بهما في السبع

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Nidāʾ ordinarily means raising and projecting the voice, but Raghib allows it to mean any sound or any sign indicating something.
rows.anchor: وقد يقال لمجرد الصوت بل لكل ما يدل على شيء وإن لم يكن صوتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here nidāʾ means supplication privately made and unheard by people, perhaps in the middle of the night; secrecy better protects sincerity and avoids ostentation, reproach, and harm from his relatives.
rows.anchor: مستورا عن الناس لم يسمعه أحد منهم حيث لم يكونوا حاضريه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Secrecy need not mean a quiet voice: he could call loudly where nobody could see or hear him; alternatively hiddenness is a figure for sincerity and lack of ostentation.
rows.anchor: ومن رفع صوته في مكان ليس بمرأى ولا مسمع من الناس فقد أخفاه

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf regards the phrase as a figure with literal secrecy also intended: concealment itself was desired, while sincerity was the chief purpose.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشف أن الأشبه أنه كناية مع إرادة الحقيقة لأن الخفاء في نفسه مطلوب أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His call may have been hidden because his voice weakened with age, as a saying describes an old person’s voice as faint and hearing as intermittent.
rows.anchor: لضعف صوته بسبب كبره كما قيل الشيخ صوته خفات وسمعه تارات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reported ages range from sixty to 120 years; 120 best fits the explanation that age weakened his voice.
rows.anchor: وقيل : كان سنه حينئذ ستين سنة وقيل خمسا وستين وقيل سبعين وقيل خمسا وسبعين وقيل ثمانين وقيل خمسا وثمانين وقيل اثنتين وتسعين

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some infer from the shortened vocative rabb that the private call was made without raising the voice; the sentence explains the call and has no independent syntactic position.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أنه أشير إلى كون النداء خفيا ليس فيه رفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Weakness is assigned to bone because it supports the body: once it fails, the rest weakens and collapses; the wording is an allusion with implicit comparison, or without comparison because bone is the strongest part.
rows.anchor: وإسناد ذلك إلى العظم لما أنه عماد البدن ودعام الجسد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari and many investigators prefer singular ʿaẓm as a generic noun, emphasizing that the body’s main support has weakened; another view says it distributes weakness to every bone, which Alusi says is inferior.
rows.anchor: وأفرد على ما قاله العلامة الزمخشري وارتضاه كثير من المحققين

rows.speaker: السكاكي
rows.claim: Al-Sakkaki says singular bone distributes weakness to each individual bone; many consider this explanation weaker because the plural could imply only some bones.
rows.anchor: وقال السكاكي : إنه ترك جمع ( العظم ) إلى الإفراد لطلب شمول الوهن

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says Zakariya complained that his molars had fallen, but Alusi says this needs a report because the verse itself does not clearly imply it.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة أنه عليه السلام اشتكى سقوط الأضراس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Minni depends on an implied predicate and describes the bone; minni rather than ʿaẓmī gives detail after generality and more clearly marks the generic sense.
rows.anchor: متعلق بمحذوف وهو حال من العظم ولم يقل عظمي

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash reads wahan with kasra on hāʾ; a ḍamma reading is also reported.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش ( وهن ) بكسر الهاء وقريء بضمها أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spreading whiteness of gray hair is likened to a bright flame; the wording combines an explicit derivative metaphor with an implicit metaphor.
rows.anchor: شبه الشيب في البياض والإنارة بشواظ النار وانتشاره في الشعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He favors the view that the explicit and implicit metaphors need not include an imagined metaphor; forcing one or treating the image as a parable is strained.
rows.anchor: وانفكاكها عن التخييلية مما عليه المحققون من أهل المعاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The action is predicated of the scalp, where hair grows, and shayban is a discriminating accusative intensifying total spread; predicating fire of a house means all inside burns.
rows.anchor: وأسند الإشتغال إلى محل الشعر ومنبته وأخرج مخرج التمييز للمبالغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shayban is not a verbal noun for shāba or a circumstantial adjective meaning gray-haired; Alusi rejects both parses.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن ( شيبا ) نصب على المصدرية لأن المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article substitutes for possessive construction because definiteness supplies its force; the earlier bone was generic, so the text adds minni.
rows.anchor: واكتفي باللام عن الإضافة لأن تعريف العهد المقصود يفيد ما تفيده

rows.speaker: ابن دريد
rows.claim: Ibn Durayd echoes the image in a line about white hair igniting among black hair.
rows.anchor: ومنها أخذ ابن دريد قوله : واشتعل المبيض في مسوده مثل اشتعال النار

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu ʿAmr assimilates the sīn into the following shīn.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي عمرو أنه أدغم السين في الشين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakariya says that throughout his long life, prayer to God was answered; the clause coordinates with what precedes and appeals to God’s established kindness.
rows.anchor: أي لم أكن بدعائي إياك خائبا في وقت من أوقات هذا العمر الطويل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi calls it strange to construe the clause as circumstantial meaning his head was already gray; the more natural reading is direct supplication.
rows.anchor: وقيل حال من ياء المتكلم إذ المعنى واشتعل رأسي وهو غريب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: An alternative, also reported from Ibn Abbas, says he was never wretched when God called him to obedience; Alusi prefers the prayer-as-supplication reading.
rows.anchor: وقيل المعنى ولم أكن بدعائك إياي إلى الطاعة شقيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He appeals to God’s long-standing habit of answering, after first recalling his old age and weakness; the appeal points to divine generosity toward the needy.
rows.anchor: وهذا توسل منه عليه السلام بما سلف منه تعالى من الاستجابة عند كل دعوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Invoking God as rabbī, with the title between kāna and its predicate, intensifies the plea; reports say God answers the servant who calls Him Lord, and Moses was told this applies to all such callers.
rows.anchor: والتعرض في الموضعين لوصف الربوبية المنبئة عن إضافة ما فيه صلاح المربوب

rows.speaker: حاتم الطائي
rows.claim: A story attributed either to Hatim al-Taʾi or Maʿn ibn Zaʾida has a needy man recall prior kindness; the host welcomes one who invokes them through their favor and grants the request.
rows.anchor: حكى حاتما الطائي وقيل معن بن زائدة أتاه محتاج فسأله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid explain al-mawālī as a man’s agnates; al-Asamm says paternal cousins, while another view includes relatives generally who manage his affairs.
rows.anchor: هم عصبة الرجل على ما روي عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما ومجاهد

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Asamm identifies the mawālī as paternal cousins who are near in lineage.
rows.anchor: وعن الأصم أنهم بنو العم وهم الذين يلونه في النسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whichever kinship sense is chosen, they were wicked Israelites, and Zakariya feared they would fail to succeed him in leading his community.
rows.anchor: وكانوا على سائر الأقوال شرار بني إسرائيل فخاف عليه السلام أن لا يحسنوا خلافته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interpreters known to Alusi agree that min warāʾī means after my death; the phrase refers to the successors’ conduct or wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: فإن المراد منه بإجماع من علمنا من المفسرين من بعد موتي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari will not attach min warāʾī to khift, since that would make the fear occur after death; Alusi considers that attachment invalid.
rows.anchor: ولم يجوز الزمخشري تعلقه بخفت لفساد المعنى

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinni parses min warāʾī as a prospective circumstantial from al-mawālī.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جني : هو حال مقدرة من ( الموالي )

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir reads wa-min warāʾī with a shortened form and fatḥa on yāʾ, like ʿaṣāy.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن كثير أنه قرأ ( ومن وراي ) بالقصر وفتح الياي كعصاي

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhri reads al-mawālī with a still yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الزهري ( الموالي ) بسكون الياء

rows.speaker: الوليد بن مسلم
rows.claim: A group including Uthman, Ibn Abbas, Zayd, Ali ibn al-Husayn, and others reads khiffat al-mawālī: the successors were few and unable, or capable predecessors died before Zakariya.
rows.anchor: الوليد بن مسلم لابن عامر ( خفت ) بفتح الخاء والفاء مشددة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿĀqir means infertile, whether the noun ʿaqr has fatḥa or ḍamma; the adjective applies to men and women, and she had been unable to bear since youth.
rows.anchor: أي لا تلد من حين شبابها إلى شيبها فالعقر بالفتح والضم العقم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both prepositional phrases in min ladunka attach to grant, with min indicating figurative origin; alternatively ladunka modifies an implied circumstantial phrase for the object.
rows.anchor: كلا الجارين متعلق بهب واللام صلة له ومن لابتداء الغاية مجازا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request is for a child from his own line, granted through pure divine favor and extraordinary power outside ordinary causes; an heir who need not be a child is possible but rejected.
rows.anchor: أعطني من محض فضلك الواسع وقدرتك الباهرة بطريق الاختراع لا بواسطة الأسباب العادية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats min ladunka as emphasizing that the requested successor be pleasing; Alusi says this is untenable.
rows.anchor: وزعم الزمخشري أن ( من لدنك ) تأكيد لكونه وليا مرضيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The delayed object spotlights the extraordinary manner of the gift and builds anticipation; placing the long description elsewhere would weaken the Quranic arrangement.
rows.anchor: تأخير المفعول على الجارين لإظهار كمال الاعتناء بكون الهبة له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Age, weakness, and the wife’s barrenness end hope through ordinary means, prompting a request for an extraordinary gift; the alternative focuses on the wife’s condition alone.
rows.anchor: فإن ما ذكره عليه السلام من كبر السن وضعف القوى وعقر المرأة موجب لانقطاع رجائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maryam’s miracles also prompted Zakariya’s prayer; their omission here is supplied by the other passage, a Quranic practice of mentioning material in one place and relying on it elsewhere.
rows.anchor: من مشاهدته عليه السلام للخوارق الظاهرة في حق مريم كما يعرب عنه قوله تعالى ( هنالك دعا زكريا ربه )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inheritance clauses most naturally modify walī; warithahu and waritha minhu are equivalent constructions, though min can be partitive, and a man’s āl includes kin, companions, or co-religionists.
rows.anchor: صفة لوليا كما هو المتبادر من الجمل الواقعة بعد النكرات

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi identifies Yaqub as Jacob son of Isaac son of Abraham, tracing Zakariya through Harun and Levi and Maryam through Solomon, David, and Judah.
rows.anchor: يعقوب على ما روي عن السدي هو يعقوب بن إسحاق بن إبراهيم

rows.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi and Muqatil identify him as Yaqub ibn Matan, brother of Imran ibn Matan, Maryam’s father; another view says he was Zakariya’s brother.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي ومقاتل : هو يعقوب بن ماثان وأخوه عمران بن ماثان أبو مريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view understands both inheritances as knowledge; al-Kalbi instead says Zakariya led the priests and wanted his son to inherit that office and the kingship of the Matan family.
rows.anchor: والمراد من الوراثة في الموضعين العلم على ما قيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes the first inheritance as prophecy and the second as kingship; radhiyyan can mean pleasing, contented, or pleasing among people, changing whether the prayer repeats or adds a request.
rows.anchor: وقيل الوراثة الأولى وراثة النبوة والثانية وراثة الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading radhiyyan as pleasing fits a request that God enable him to act well, complementing the request for knowledge; placing rabb between the two parts intensifies the plea.
rows.anchor: وعلى ما قلنا يكون دعاء بتوفيقه للعمل كما أن الأول متضمن للدعاء بتوفيقه للعلم

rows.speaker: السكاكي
rows.claim: Al-Sakkaki makes the two inheritance clauses independent explanatory sentences rather than modifiers of walī, to avoid implying Yahya died before Zakariya.
rows.anchor: واختار السكاكي أن الجملتين مستأنفتان استئنافا بيانيا

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf replies that reports conflict and most say Zakariya died before Yahya; it rejects partial unanswered prayer because Quran says the request was answered and context supports the whole request.
rows.anchor: والأكثر على هلاك زكريا قبله عليهما السلام

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say inheritance of knowledge avoids a problem if Yahya died first because he transmitted it and left an enduring legacy; Alusi objects that an heir ordinarily outlives the deceased.
rows.anchor: حيث كان المراد من الوراثة هنا وراثة العلم لا يضر هلاكه قبل أبيه

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو والكسائي
rows.claim: Abu Amr, al-Kisai, al-Zuhri, al-Aʿmash, Talha and others read both verbs jussive as responses to prayer: if granted a child, he will inherit, expressing expectation.
rows.anchor: بجزم الفعلين على أنهما جواب الدعاء والمعنى أن تهب لي ذلك يرثني

rows.speaker: علي وابن عباس وجعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: Ali, Ibn Abbas, Jaʿfar al-Sadiq, al-Hasan and others read the verbs nominative: the child inherits knowledge, while Zakariya inherits kingship through the child’s elevation; the conjunction may be simple or circumstantial.
rows.anchor: قرأ علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه وابن عباس وجعفر بن محمد رضي الله تعالى عنهم

rows.speaker: صاحب اللوامح
rows.claim: The author of al-Lawamiʿ proposes fronting: give me a child from Jacob’s house who inherits prophecy if I die first, and whose wealth I inherit if he dies first; Alusi signals a later objection.
rows.anchor: فهب لي وليا من آل يعقوب يرثني النبوة إن مت قبله وأرثه ماله إن مات قبلي

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A further reading makes arithu an active participle subject of yarithuni: one walī is generated from another, as in saying I saw a lion from him.
rows.anchor: يرثني ولي من ذلك الولي أو به فقد جرد من الولي وليا

rows.speaker: الجحدري
rows.claim: Al-Jahdari is also reported to incline the wāw in arithu.
rows.anchor: وعن الجحدري أنه قرأ ( وأرث ) بإمالة الواو

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid reads a diminutive form meaning little heir; Alusi explains its morphology and suggests it may mark the child’s youth, though the proposed laudatory sense is less apt.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد ( أو يرث ) تصغير وارث وأصله وويرث بواوين

rows.speaker: الشيعة
rows.claim: Shiʿi interpreters argue from the verse that prophets leave property, taking inheritance in its literal financial sense; Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima, and Abu Salih are reported to gloss it as my wealth.
rows.anchor: استدل الشيعة بالآية على أن الأنبياء عليهم السلام تورث عنهم أموالهم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: A report through al-Hasan attributes to the Prophet a prayer for Zakariya and a question about what heirs he had; a variant asks who would inherit his property.
rows.anchor: عن الحسن أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم قال في الآية : يرحم الله تعالى أخي زكريا

rows.speaker: أهل السنة
rows.claim: Alusi says Sunni doctrine, based on reports they judge sound, is that prophets leave no property and it is not inherited.
rows.anchor: ومذهب أهل السنة أن الأنبياء عليهم السلام لا يورثون مالا ولا يورثون

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some argue against prophecy as the inheritance because that makes the prayer that Yahya be pleasing redundant, and against knowledge because it is acquired rather than inherited.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز ههنا حملها على وراثة النبوة

rows.speaker: جعفر الصادق
rows.claim: Al-Kulayni transmits Jaʿfar al-Sadiq saying scholars inherit prophets: prophets left neither coins nor dirhams but traditions, and whoever takes them gains a great share.
rows.anchor: إن العلماء ورثة الأنبياء وذلك أن الأنبياء لم يورثوا درهما ولا دينارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inheritance can encompass knowledge, office, and wealth; jurists’ customary usage narrowed it to money, while the Quran commonly uses it for nonmaterial inheritance, making that usage established.
rows.anchor: بل هي حقيقة فيما يعم وراثة العلم والمنصب والمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reason to interpret the verse nonfinancially is to protect a prophet’s truthful speech; reports that prophets leave property are unreliable by hadith criticism.
rows.anchor: الداعي متحقق وهي صيانة قول المعصوم عن الكذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi rejects the objections about prophetic inheritance and acquired knowledge; Jaʿfar’s reports call scholars heirs and say Solomon inherited David and Muhammad inherited Solomon in knowledge and prophecy.
rows.anchor: فقد تعلقت الوراثة بما ليس بكسبي في كلام الصادق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A purified soul such as Zakariya’s has no worldly appetite; he could not have feared or grieved over ordinary property passing to bad relatives or sought a child for that reason.
rows.anchor: فإنه كان مشهورا بكمال الانقطاع والتجرد فيستحيل عادة أن يخاف من وراثة المال

rows.speaker: الشيعة
rows.claim: Shiʿi interpreters say Zakariya feared his cousins would spend the estate badly and requested a righteous heir; Alusi says the successor, not the deceased, is responsible for its use.
rows.anchor: وقالت الشيعة : إنه عليه السلام خاف أن يصرف بنوعمه ماله بعد موته فيما لا ينبغي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakariya could have donated the estate before death and left wicked cousins nothing; Shiʿi claims that prophets know and choose their death time also remove fear of sudden death.
rows.anchor: بأن يصرفه قبل موته ويتصدق به كله في سبيل الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakariya sought a child to uphold divine law and continue prophecy among his descendants, bringing multiplied reward over time.
rows.anchor: فليس قصده عليه السلام من مسئلة الولد سوى إجراء أحكام الله تعالى وترويج الشريعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address is introduced as speech delivered through an angel, who conveys the divine wording for the Prophet to recount, as in the command to say My servants.
rows.anchor: لكن لا بأن يخاطبه سبحانه وتعالى بذلك بالذات بل بواسطة الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The glad tidings answer Zakariya’s call and promise its fulfillment; the delay does not conflict with a prompt response, since the promise itself may count as fulfillment.
rows.anchor: وهذا جواب لندائه عليه السلام ووعد بإجابة دعائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common account has the announcement shortly after the prayer and birth within months; other reports place birth forty or sixty years later.
rows.anchor: والمشهور أن هذا القول كان إثر الدعاء ولم يكن بين البشارة والولادة إلا أشهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghulām means a male child, though the feminine ghulāma is also used.
rows.anchor: والغلام الولد الذكر وقد يقال للأنثى : غلامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naming Yahya reinforces the promise and honors him; Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi, and Ibn Aslam say no one before bore the same name.
rows.anchor: وفي تعيين اسمه عليه السلام تأكيد للوعد وتشريف له عليه السلام

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says rare names were favored because they attract notice and stand out; a poem praises unusual names, and Salt ibn Ata cited his foreign name among traits that advanced him.
rows.anchor: وهذا كما قال الزمخشري شاهد على أن الأسماء النادرة التي لا يكاد الناس يستعملونها

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid, Ata, and Ibn Jubayr take samiyyan to mean equal or similar: Yahya had no equal because he neither sinned nor even intended sin.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد أن ( سميا ) بمعنى شبيها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The Prophet says every descendant of Adam erred or intended error except Yahya, who neither intended nor committed sin; Alusi says reports on this are numerous.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : ما من أحد من ولد آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations say Yahya had no equal because he was born to an old man and a barren old woman, or because he embodied the qualities named elsewhere: confirmer, leader, chaste, and righteous prophet.
rows.anchor: وقيل : لم يكن له شبيه لذلك ولأنه ولد بين شيخ فان وعجوز عاقر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quranic question whether God has a namesake supports the counterpart sense; Alusi’s strongest view is that Yahya is a foreign name because Arabs did not typically name children with Arabic words.
rows.anchor: ومن هذا الإطلاق قوله تعالى : ( هل تعلم له سميا ) لأنه الذي يقتضيه التفريع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Arabic, Yahya derives from a verb; proposed meanings include long life, revival of his mother’s womb, life between aged parents, wisdom, guidance, or martyrdom, since martyrs live.
rows.anchor: وقيل : سمي بذلك لأنه حي به رحم أمه وقيل لأنه حي بين شيخ فان وعجوز عاقر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name may signal the inheritance Zakariya requested; Arabic and foreign derivations differ in meter and diminutive form.
rows.anchor: وكان في ذلك إشارة إلى أنه عليه السلام يرث حسبما سأل زكريا عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qāla resumes the narrative after an implied question about Zakariya’s response; he calls God directly despite receiving the angel’s message, intensifying prayer and avoiding any suggestion that divine knowledge depends on mediation.
rows.anchor: استئناف مبني على السؤال كأنه قيل فماذا قال عليه السلام حينئذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anna can mean how or from where; kāna may be complete with the prepositional phrase attached to it, or defective with different placements for anna and lī.
rows.anchor: كلمة ( أنى ) بمعنى كيف أو من أين وكان أما تامة وأنى واللام متعلقان بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His wife’s barrenness and his reaching extreme age are circumstantial clauses with an implied qad; min marks the starting point, and ʿatiyy means dryness and hardening in joints and bones or a state beyond remedy.
rows.anchor: والعتي من عتى يعتو اليبس والقحول في المفاصل والعظام

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Raghib defines ʿatiyy as a condition that cannot be corrected or cured, illustrated by a poet’s line that training old age is a hardship.
rows.anchor: هو حالة لا سبيل إلى إصلاحها ومداواتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form derives from a root with two wāws; their sequence and heavy vowels lead to yāʾ substitutions and a kasra on ʿayn.
rows.anchor: وأصله عتوو كقعود فاستثقل توالي الضمتين والواوين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wife was reportedly 98 years old.
rows.anchor: وأما عمر امرأته فقد قيل إنه كان ثماني وتسعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min in min al-kibar may be partitive, marking a stage of old age called ʿatiyy, or explanatory; it modifies the verb or serves as a circumstantial phrase.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن تكون ( من ) للتبعيض أي بلغت من مدارج الكبر ومراتبه ما يسمى عتيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This parallels Zakariya’s statement in Aal Imran that old age reached him, with a different grammatical perspective; each passage’s wording has its rhetorical point.
rows.anchor: وأصل المعنى متحد مع قوله تعالى في آل عمران حكاية عنه بلغني الكبر

rows.speaker: الإرشاد
rows.claim: Al-Irshad explains the reversed order of barrenness and Zakariya’s age: his age was already mentioned in the prayer here, while it had not been mentioned in the Aal Imran prayer, so his condition came first there.
rows.anchor: وفي إرشاد العقل السليم لعل ذلك لما أنه قد ذكر حاله في تضاعيف دعائه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another explanation is that prayer and dialogue happened more than once, with varied order for stylistic variety and each passage supplying what the other omits.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : يحتمل تكرر الدعاء والمحاورة واختلاف الأسلوب للتفنن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakariya apparently did not consider himself infertile, so he names age as his obstacle and his wife as barren; he asks in wonder at God’s power and recognizes pure favor, not doubt.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه عليه السلام كان يعرف من نفسه أنه لم يكن عاقرا ولذلك ذكر الكبر

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: An alternative takes the question as apparent improbability voiced for disbelievers to remove their objection; he may have later spoken aloud to manifest the blessing.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هو استبعاد لكنه ليس راجعا إلى المتكلم بل هو بالنسبة إلى المبطلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The view that Zakariya himself doubted because sixty years passed and he forgot his prayer is very far-fetched.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هو استبعاد راجع إلى المتكلم حيث كان بين الدعاء والبشارة ستون سنة

rows.speaker: الانتصاف
rows.claim: Al-Intisaf says Zakariya asked generally for a child, without specifying that he and his wife would remain old and barren; he may expect renewed strength or another mother. Alusi objects that grant me a successor implies a child despite their condition.
rows.anchor: وقال في الانتصاف : الظاهر والله تعالى أعلم أن زكريا عليه السلام طلب ولدا على الجملة
